style: Brief, warm offline commentary; discoveries describe recorded play, introductions use the existing sourced field guide.

s2.text: You are an orange coral goby. A coral colony can provide both shelter and food.

s0.text: You are a silver sprat. These little fish gather in great, shimmering schools.

s11.text: You are a peach fairy basslet. Males and females have different colors and fin shapes.

s30.text: You are a humbug damselfish. Branching coral offers shelter between trips for drifting plankton.

s45.text: You are a banded coral shrimp. Long white antennae help attract fish to its cleaning services.

s1.text: You are a neon damselfish. Look for its brilliant blue body and yellow tail.

s13.text: You are a Banggai cardinalfish. These small fish come from sheltered waters around Indonesia’s Banggai islands.

s43.text: You are a cleaner wrasse. Removing parasites gives the cleaner food and helps its visiting clients.

s58.text: You are a purple anthias. These colorful fish gather along drop-offs and steep reef slopes.

s7.text: You are an anemonefish. Its mucus coating helps it live among an anemone’s stinging tentacles.

s3.text: You are a royal gramma. These reef fish live close to caves and overhanging ledges.

s53.text: You are a flashlight fish. Living bacteria beneath its eyes provide light that the fish can reveal.

s10.text: You are a sixbar wrasse. This little reef fish searches for a varied collection of small meals.

s6.text: You are a longnose butterflyfish. Its narrow snout reaches toward small foods around the reef.

s57.text: You are our checkerboard hawkfish. This game character explores the reef from quiet watching places.

s31.text: You are a whitespot hawkfish. Small fish and crustaceans make up its main meals near the reef.

s9.text: You are a yellow goatfish. Its whisker-like barbels explore the sand by touch and taste.

s12.text: You are a squirrelfish. Large eyes help these nighttime hunters explore after sheltering by day.

s42.text: You are a yellowtail fusilier. Large schools feed on tiny animal plankton in midwater.

s54.text: You are a painted frogfish. Its colors vary so much that color alone cannot identify it.

s5.text: You are a palette surgeonfish. Tiny plankton and growing algae both belong on its menu.

s56.text: You are a longfin bannerfish. Its meals include drifting plankton and small animals on the bottom.

s4.text: You are a Moorish idol. Larger idols often travel in small groups around the reef.

s52.text: You are a pencilled rabbitfish. They graze algae, seaweed and seagrass, in pairs or schools.

s8.text: You are a foxface rabbitfish. Young foxfaces school together, while larger fish can form pairs.

s23.text: You are a longhorn cowfish. It blows water at sand to uncover little animals beneath.

s25.text: You are a regal angelfish. Sponges and tunicates are animals, and part of its natural menu.

s48.text: You are an orange-spotted filefish. Branching coral provides its natural food and nighttime shelter.

s22.text: You are a spotted pufferfish. Individuals can look quite different, even when they belong to the same species.

s19.text: You are a cuttlefish. Changing colors and skin textures can help cuttlefishes disappear against their surroundings.

s40.text: You are a longfin batfish. Its especially tall juvenile fins change proportion as it grows.

s14.text: You are an oriental sweetlip. Its meals include little animals living on the seabed.

s24.text: You are a clown triggerfish. Pale body spots and yellow around the mouth help identify it.

s20.text: You are a lionfish. Broad, fan-like fins and separate spines make its silhouette distinctive.

s21.text: You are a devil scorpionfish. Bright colors hidden inside its fins can startle an approaching predator.

s15.text: You are a parrotfish. Many parrotfishes bite reef surfaces with teeth joined into a beak.

s50.text: You are a yellowspot emperor. Look for the bright yellow blotch below its rear dorsal fin.

s16.text: You are a coral grouper. Look for the bright blue spots on its orange-red body.

s41.text: You are a trumpetfish. A larger neighbor can become moving cover for its approach to a meal.

s37.text: You are an electric ray. This flattened Australian ray often waits buried in sand or mud.

s51.text: You are a golden snapper. Even silty coastal water can hold a rich collection of small meals.

s39.text: You are a coral trout. Fishes and crustaceans are on this spotted grouper’s menu.

s27.text: You are a blue-spotted stingray. Sandy areas beside reefs offer worms, shrimp and other small meals.

s59.text: You are a longsnout flathead. Its low, broad head can rest partly buried in sandy reef areas.

s18.text: You are a crocodile needlefish. Its long, toothed jaws hunt small fish near the surface.

s55.text: You are a silver trevally. These schooling fish use reefs and nearby sand in southern waters.

s28.text: You are a rainbow runner. Even a large, fast swimmer can depend on tiny animals for food.

s26.text: You are a whitemouth moray. White spots, a pale mouth and a yellow tail tip help identify it.

s49.text: You are a doublelined mackerel. Dense schools gather near reefs and feed on fish and crustaceans.

s29.text: You are a humphead wrasse. These long-lived reef fish take years to mature.

s17.text: You are a blackfin barracuda. Dark bars and a deeply forked tail mark this large reef fish.

s33.text: You are a whitetip reef shark. Unlike some sharks, it can breathe while resting in a cave.

s36.text: You are a wobbegong. Carpet sharks often rest on sandy or rocky bottoms and feed at night.

s32.text: You are a blacktip reef shark. These sharks often stay close to familiar, shallow reef areas.

s38.text: You are a giant grouper. A large individual may hover quietly or remain still on the bottom.

s35.text: You are a tiger shark. A varied diet and occasional bursts of speed suit its hunting life.

s34.text: You are a great white shark. Its powerful body and crescent-shaped tail suit coastal and offshore waters.

sprat-feeding-wave.text: A shared meal, then together again. You and your sprat neighbors found food without leaving the school behind.

damsel-territory.text: Back at your familiar coral. A feeding excursion and a safe return make a little circuit through the reef.

coral-home.text: Home again. You found a meal and returned to the same coral refuge.

gramma-ledge.text: Back beneath the ledge. Even a short feeding trip can end in a familiar sheltered place.

idol-browsing-group.text: Sponge, algae, and company again. Your Moorish idol explored different feeding places before finding a fellow browser.

surgeonfish-route.text: There is new growth at your first patch. Moving between meals gave this little garden time to recover.

butterflyfish-crevices.text: Two small feeding places explored. Your narrow snout helped you investigate the reef’s little crevices.

anemone-partner.text: Back among the tentacles. Your feeding trip ended at the same living anemone you chose as home.

foxface-companion.text: Both foxfaces fed, then met again. Making room for a neighbor became part of your own feeding trip.

sand-neighbors.text: Your sand search helped a neighbor too. A hidden meal became a discovery that another forager could share.

wrasse-search.text: A worm, then a shrimp. Searching different little places brought your wrasse a varied meal.

basslet-feeding-wave.text: Your basslet neighbors fed and regrouped. The feeding patch was a stop along the school’s shared journey.

squirrelfish-night-trip.text: Back to your nighttime refuge. Two different crustacean meals made a quiet trip through the dark.

cardinalfish-cover.text: A short trip from cover, then home. Your cardinalfish did not need a long chase to find food.

sweetlip-bottom-route.text: Two bottom patches explored. Your sweetlip found different small meals along the seabed.

parrotfish-route.text: Your first grazing patch is growing again. A circuit around the reef can give yesterday’s meal time to renew.

grouper-ambush.text: A patient wait became a meal. Your grouper let its prey come close before making a short strike.

barracuda-pursuit.text: A burst, a meal, and a quiet return. Your barracuda’s pursuit was one part of a longer patrol.

needlefish-surface.text: Back along the upper water. Your needlefish found a small meal near its chosen surface route.

changing-colors.text: Sand and mottled reef, two different disguises. Your cuttlefish changed its pattern to match the places it explored.

lionfish-watch.text: A careful approach, then back to the ledge. Your lionfish watched its meal before making the feeding trip.

scorpionfish-ambush.text: Stillness, then a sudden strike. Your scorpionfish found a meal by waiting close to the bottom.

puffer-shell-meal.text: A hard shell and a softer sponge. Your puffer explored two very different kinds of feeding place.

sand-search.text: Two meals uncovered beneath the sand. A little water from your cowfish revealed food that was hidden before.

triggerfish-hard-prey.text: A crab and a snail opened. Your triggerfish’s strong mouth helped with two armored meals.

angelfish-quiet-browse.text: Sponge, algae, then quiet cover. Your angelfish returned from its browsing trip to a sheltered place.

moray-cave-trip.text: Back inside your chosen cave. Your moray made a feeding excursion and returned to rest.

stingray-sifting.text: Shrimp and worms found below. Your stingray searched two different patches along the bottom.

runner-speed-trip.text: A quick pursuit, then room to recover. Your rainbow runner returned to its route after a real meal.

humphead-hard-prey.text: Two armored meals explored. Your humphead wrasse handled a snail and a crab on this feeding trip.

humbug-coral-trip.text: After a plankton meal, your humbug damselfish is back among the coral branches of its chosen refuge.

hawkfish-perch.text: Back on your lookout. Your hawkfish watched a meal, fed nearby, and returned to its reef perch.

blacktip-reef-edge.text: A meal at the reef edge, then around again. Your blacktip returned to the route it surveyed.

whitetip-rest-trip.text: Resting again after a feeding trip. Your whitetip found a meal and returned to its chosen ledge.

white-shark-meal.text: A substantial meal, then back to open water. Your white shark completed the route it chose to explore.

tiger-varied-route.text: Fish and crab along one route. Your tiger shark explored two different kinds of hunting ground.

wobbegong-bottom.text: The bottom became a watching place. Your wobbegong waited, noticed a meal, then made a short feeding trip.

electric-ray-watch.text: A bottom meal, then rest. Your electric ray is back at its chosen watching place.

giant-grouper-watch.text: A quiet watch from a broad ledge. Your giant grouper made a feeding trip and returned to the same place.

trout-reef-trip.text: Out from the reef and back again. Your coral trout found a small fish along its surveyed route.

batfish-loose-browsing.text: Two browsers fed, then reunited. Your batfish shared a trip across algae and drifting plankton.

trumpetfish-moving-cover.text: Your neighbor became moving cover. Your trumpetfish followed, found a meal, and returned to that same companion.

school-life.text: A meal, then back in the school. Your fusilier found its companions again after the feeding excursion.

reef-helper.text: Three kinds of client helped. Your cleaner wrasse found food while removing parasites from other reef fish.

seahorse-holdfast-meal.text: A meal from a holdfast, then rest. The seahorse took food and settled among the plants.

night-helper.text: Three kinds of nighttime visitor helped. Your cleaner shrimp’s claws made a difference to other reef neighbors.

crab-detritus-walk.text: A small scavenger carries on. The crab handled its meal, then continued along the bottom.

sea-star-bottom-meal.text: A quiet meal on the reef. The sea star finished feeding and settled to digest.

filefish-companion.text: Both filefish browsed, then met again. You made room for a companion during your shared feeding trip.

mackerel-pursuit.text: A burst of speed, then a breather. Your mackerel returned to its route after pursuing a meal.

emperor-bottom-hunt.text: A bottom crab and a swimming fish. Your emperor explored two very different meals on one trip.

snapper-two-visits.text: Two watched visits in the dark. A return to the lookout connected your shrimp and fish meals.

rabbitfish-companion.text: A shared feeding trip, then together again. Both rabbitfish had room to browse before reuniting.

flashlight-night-excursion.text: Light in the dark, then together again. Your flashlight fish fed and returned to its nighttime companion.

frogfish-ambush.text: A lure, a visitor, and a short strike. Your frogfish’s patient ambush became a meal.

trevally-feeding-route.text: Across two feeding grounds and back. Your trevally found shrimp and fish along its chosen route.

bannerfish-mixed-trip.text: Floating food and a bottom visit. Both bannerfish fed before finding one another again.

hawkfish-lookouts.text: A second lookout found. Your hawkfish fed from one perch, then settled at a different watching place.

anthias-feeding-wave.text: Your anthias neighbors fed and regrouped. The school’s shared trip connected a meal with a return to company.

flathead-ambush.text: A quiet surprise above the sand. Your flathead waited until a small fish came close before striking.

nudibranch-browsing.text: Along the sponge garden. You watched a nudibranch browse, then continue its slow route across the reef.

snail-grazing.text: A grazing trail continues. You noticed a snail take algae, then move onward along the reef.

urchin-night-graze.text: A grazer after dark. You watched an urchin feed on algae and settle again.

anemone-passing-food.text: Food at an attached home. You watched an anemone take a meal, then relax its tentacles.

reef-clinic.text: A familiar face at your clinic. Gentle care helped two visitors, and one came back to greet you.

disappearing-artist.text: Three disguises discovered. Matching sand, shade, and mottled rock helped you hide from a passing fish.

sandcastle-engineer.text: Your grazing left sand behind. Resting a patch let its algae renew, and another fish found a meal.

whisker-detective.text: A discovery worth sharing. Your barbels found a buried meal, and a reef neighbor enjoyed it.

cardinalfish-nursery.text: A quiet nursery for your young. Their father carried the brood in his mouth until they were ready.

helper.text: A helping fin. Your cleaning has made another reef fish feel better.

meal.text: A first good meal. You found suitable food when your fish needed energy.

clean.text: Fresh again. A completed cleaner visit removed parasites from your fish.

shelter.text: Safe harbour. Your fish spent a quiet moment hidden in a shelter that fits.

care1.text: Your first care stamp. A species stayed fed and healthy with your help.

care3.text: Three species well cared for. Your growing journal remembers each one.

play3.text: Three different lives explored. Each species offers another way to see the reef.

play10.text: Ten different lives explored. Your journal is becoming a collection of reef perspectives.

visit3.text: Three habitats visited. Different corners of the atoll are becoming familiar.

visit9.text: Around the atoll. All nine habitats are now part of your journal.

discovery1.text: Your first way of living discovered. A small reef story now has a place in your journal.

discovery5.text: Five ways of living discovered. Your careful observations are building a richer picture of the reef.

discovery15.text: Fifteen ways of living discovered. Your journal holds many different rhythms of reef life.

night.text: A meal after dark. Your fish found needed food beneath the nighttime water.

neighbor.text: Good neighbors. You noticed another fish receiving a cleaner’s help.

school.text: A guest in the school. Your fish spent time swimming beside its companions.
